MR. CHAIRMAN: Now, Question No. 20.  
Present status of UDAN Scheme 
*20.    SHRI HARSH MAHAJAN: Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased to  
state: 
(a)   present status of UDAN Scheme in the country and major objectives of the 
Scheme at this stage; 
(b)     proposals envisaged under UDAN Scheme for the State of Himachal Pradesh, 
including development/expansion of airports and heliports and the 
commencement or expansion of fixed-wing aircraft and helicopter services; 
(c)   whether Government is aware that regular flight services are not being operated 
from Shimla airport in Himachal Pradesh under UDAN Scheme and, if so, the 
reasons therefor; and 
(d)   concrete steps being taken by Government to commence regular flight services 
from Shimla airport at the earliest and whether any timeline has been fixed in 
this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI KINJARAPU RAMMOHAN  
NAIDU): A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
                                                         Statement  
(a)  The Regional Connectivity Scheme-Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik (RCS-
UDAN) was launched in 2016 with the objective of enhancing regional air connectivity 
to remote and unserved areas of the country through a demand based bidding 
mechanism that incentivizes airlines to connect unserved/underserved airstrips in the 
52
[ RAJYA SABHA ]

country. Under the Scheme, 657 RCS routes have been operationalised, connecting 
93 unserved and underserved airports, including 15 heliports and 2 water aerodromes 
as on 20.01.2026. More than 160 Lakhs passengers benefitted by connecting through 
3.36 Lakhs RCS flights operated under the scheme.  
(b)  Under the UDAN scheme, two airports and nine helipads have been 
identified in the state of Himachal Pradesh for development and operation of RCS 
flights. A total of 38 RCS routes have been operationalised, connecting 6 (six) 
aerodromes namely Shimla, Kullu, Rampur (Heliport), Mandi (Heliport), Reckong 
Peo (Heliport) & Sanjoli (Heliport) in the State of Himachal Pradesh. 
(c) and (d)  M/s Alliance Air operated flight services on the Shimla-Delhi-
Shimla and Shimla-Amritsar-Shimla routes under the RCS-UDAN using ATR-42 
aircraft. However, operations on the Delhi sector were discontinued effective from 
16th October, 2025, following the completion of the prescribed three-year Viability 
Gap Funding (VGF) tenure, while the Amritsar service, which commenced on 
November 16, 2023, was discontinued with effect from October 17, 2025, due to a 
shortage of operational aircraft in the airline's fleet. 
If any airline submits a valid bid for the RCS routes connecting Shimla airport, 
in the upcoming rounds of bidding, the same may be considered as per the 
provisions of the UDAN Scheme. 
Further, the Government has announced the launch of the modified UDAN 
Scheme to increase regional connectivity to 120 new destinations across the country, 
to cater to 4 crore passengers over the next 10 years. 
SHRI HARSH MAHAJAN: Mr. Chairman, Sir, through you, I would like to ask the hon. 
Minister whether the new modified UDAN scheme includes Shimla or not. Secondly, I 
would like to know whether the two ATRs, which were specially purchased for 
Shimla, are with Alliance Airways. If yes, why are they not operational? For what 
reasons, are they not operational? And when will this flight to Shimla start? 
MR. CHAIRMAN:  Hon. Minister.  
SHRI KINJARAPU RAMMOHAN NAIDU : Sir, the hon. Member has asked two 
questions. The first one is: Will the UDAN scheme be modified, and will the modified 
UDAN include Shimla? Sir, the UDAN scheme has revolutionised the Indian civil 
aviation sector, and we were able to extend connectivity to regional remote areas,

especially tier 2 and tier 3 cities, where we established airports, but connectivity was 
still a challenge. So, under the UDAN scheme, which was launched under the 
visionary leadership of the hon. Prime Minister, we have operationalised 657 routes, 
and 159 lakh passengers have travelled on these routes. 
So, the success of this UDAN story needs to be continued because we are in 
the plan of opening up more airports in the country. So, it is a necessity that the 
UDAN needs to be extended.  But, the good thing that we are doing right now is, 
from whatever feedback we got in these 10 years, we felt that the UDAN scheme can 
be bettered. Taking in the update from the present scenario, we are bringing in those 
changes. I am very thankful to the hon. Finance Minister, who in the last budget only 
announced that the UDAN is going to be extended. The specific things that were 
mentioned were, 120 new destinations are going to be established in the coming 10 
years and, especially, the hilly terrain, the North Eastern States and the Himalayan 
States are going to be given a priority in establishing regional connectivity. So, 
definitely, Himachal Pradesh, and to the extent Shimla, is going to be there in the 
extended UDAN also. The second thing is the ATR 42s. There are two types of ATR 
aircraft, one is the ATR 72 seater and the other is the 42 seater. Alliance Air has two 
ATR 42s. One is on the ground right now. As there are some issues, it is not 
operational. There is one which is operational, which is specifically operating in the 
Uttarakhand sector. And, Shimla being an airport which is only 1093 meters, it is very 
specific in the kind of aircraft that can operate there. It is a very small runway and the 
Shimla airport is such a way that all around the airport there is a lot of hilly terrain. So, 
when you have to land, you have to use only specific number of aircraft. The ATR 42, 
which is a 42 seater aircraft, even if it is landing there, it is with a load penalty. That 
means that you cannot operate with fully 42 seats also. This has been going on for 
some time now with the help of UDAN itself.  If I remember correctly, Shimla was one 
of the first routes which was started under UDAN also in 2016. So, that was the 
priority with which Shimla was started. UDAN is not a scheme which is going to 
continuously provide funding for eternity. It was designed in such a way that is going

familiarize the airports with the connectivity, and, then, as and when people get used, 
the commercial angle takes over and the airlines are going to start the connectivity

operations at Shimla have continued. Once the UDAN ended, the scheme was taken 
out, the operation stopped.  But, very recently, the hon. Chief Minister of Himachal

you will gain the loyalty of the world and their rule would be secure. 
Sir, our leader, Mr. M.K. Stalin, the Chief Minister, is not only a party leader, 
he is a Lieutenant. In 1982 itself, we identified him and said, he is a Lieutenant. And, 
now with our strong alliance, we are standing there. Come with all your troops. Come 
with all your battalion. As Waterloo was to Napoleon Bonaparte, Tamil Nadu will be to 
BJP. Thank you, Sir.  
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (DR. DINESH SHARMA): Next speaker is, Shri Sanjay Singh.

thank you very much for giving me opportunity to speak on the President’s Address.

ddressed both Houses. I rise to convey our gratitude for the Address delivered by

for her Address, in which she issued guidance to ensure the proper implementation of

livelihood. States such as Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, West Bengal, Karnataka, 
Punjab, and Haryana are all heavily dependent on agriculture. With a large heart, the 
hon. Prime Minister has been providing ₹6,000 every year to farmers through the PM 
Kisan Samman Nidhi scheme.  
 In para 18 of the hon. President’s Speech, it was mentioned that over 4 lakh 
crore rupees have been transferred till date to the farmers. This was mentioned in the 
hon. President's Address. The Scheme was started in 2019. It has been six years of 
implementation and only Rs. 75,000 crore per year is allocated. The amount of Rs. 
6,000 per year has remained stagnant despite significant increase in inflation since 
2019. We demand that this amount is revised to at least Rs. 9,000 so that it is 
adjusted for inflation. There is a strong need to increase it to a minimum of ₹9,000. 
Sir, there are many reasons for making this request. In Andhra Pradesh, 45 percent of 
farmers are tenant farmers and about 40 percent are small and marginal farmers. This 
means that 85 percent of farmers belong to weaker sections.  
  They all belong to weaker sections. They are from OBCs, Scheduled Castes 
and Scheduled Tribes. They are just having ten acres of land. They cultivate their own 
land. They constitute only 15 per cent. Sir, when Shri Y. S. Jagan Mohan Reddy Garu 
was the Chief Minister, many welfare schemes were implemented. Unfortunately, all 
those schemes have been stopped. As a result, farmers today have no alternative 
support. …(Interruptions)… Please do not get anxious; I am explaining. Sir, along with 
the ₹6,000 given by the hon. Prime Minister, an additional ₹7,500 was provided by the 
State Government, making it ₹13,500 per year. This continued uninterrupted for five 
years. 
Sir, the present hon. Chief Minister also promised during the elections to give 
an additional ₹20,000, that is, ₹40,000 over two years. However, instead of ₹40,000, 
only about one-fourth, around ₹10,000 has been given so far, and the remaining 
amount has not been released. This is a major breach of election promise. 
Sir, apart from this, there was a free crop insurance scheme under which the 
entire premium was paid by the Government. Small farmers, big farmers and tenant 
farmers, everyone’s premium was fully borne by the Government. This scheme was 
implemented continuously from 2019 to 2024. However, the present Government has 
shut down this scheme as well. This shutdown was done without informing the 
farmers in advance. Farmers were not informed that the scheme was being 
discontinued and that they would have to pay the premium themselves. As a result,

74 percent of farmers lost eligibility to receive crop insurance. Sir, this is extremely 
unfortunate. Had the Government informed the farmers in advance, this situation 
could have been avoided.  While 74 per cent of farmers lost insurance coverage, only 
those farmers who had taken loans from Primary Agricultural Cooperative Societies or 
commercial banks received insurance. That accounts for merely 26.6 per cent. Please 
consider the magnitude of losses suffered by farmers.  Because of these two major 
reasons, I am requesting the Central Government to increase the assistance under 
PM-KISAN Scheme. 
Sir, apart from this, free electricity is being provided. The present Government 
is also giving free electricity for nine hours. Earlier, free borewells were also provided. 
Even a small farmer owning ten acres or small farmers jointly could get a borewell 
drilled. The cost of extracting groundwater was about ₹5 lakh, which was entirely 
borne by the Government. If the borewell failed, another borewell was drilled at a 
different location, again at a cost of ₹5 lakh, fully paid by the Government.  Sir, today, 
all these schemes have now been completely stopped. Agricultural testing 
laboratories, infrastructure development like cold storage units, and other facilities 
were earlier provided with subsidies. Dairy farmers were also given a bonus of ₹4 per 
litre of milk. Today all these schemes have been completely stopped. Therefore, with 
the intention that the assistance given by the hon. Prime Minister may be enhanced 
and made more effective, I am making this request. 
Sir, when so many schemes were implemented earlier, shutting them all down 
has left farmers in a helpless condition. Agriculture is not a sector that yields profits 
every year. Andhra Pradesh is a cyclone-prone State. Every year, cyclones affect the 
Godavari Delta, Krishna Delta, Penna Delta, or North Andhra. After stopping all these 
schemes, our friends ask us, What have you done? When we explain, they should tell 
us whether what we are saying is true or not. Everything I have stated is factual. Sir, 
because all these schemes have been discontinued, we are seeking help from the 
hon. Prime Minister. What loss is there to you if assistance is given? If the hon. Prime 
Minister gives assistance with a large heart, it will benefit farmers. You and I are 
farmers; we are all connected to agriculture, directly or indirectly. It benefits everyone. 
Therefore, keeping this in mind, we are requesting the hon. Prime Minister to act 
accordingly.

Dependence on imported components means trade deficit persist, even in 
high-growth sectors like electronics. True Atmanirbhar Bharat  requires design 
capabilities are R&D, domestic supply chains, and skilled employment, not just final-
stage assembly. The Government celebrates India as a manufacturing giant, but what 
it has created is an assembly economy--high on exports, low on value addition, jobs 
and technology sovereignty.  
Yes, highways, railways and Vande Bharat  trains inspire pride.  But, 
infrastructure should unite, not divide.  While premium trains multiply, ordinary 
passengers face over-crowding, rising fares, and safety concerns. Rural roads exist 
on maps, but maintenance is poor and connectivity to schools and hospitals remain 
fragile.  Development cannot be judged only by speed; it must be judged by access. 
Next is Labour Reforms. The Labour Codes are presented as reform, but 
workers were not consulted. These Codes dilute job security, weaken collective 
bargaining, and ignore the needs of 90 per cent of work force-- informal workers, 
including domestic workers.  Reform that benefit balance-sheets, but weaken 
livelihoods cannot be called people-centric.   
Next is Youth, Startups & Skills and Aspirations Without Assurance. India’s 
youth is ambitious, talented and restless. But skill programmes cannot succeed when 
education outcomes are weak and job opportunities limited. Whether any track has 
been kept about persons getting job after the skill training. The outcome of securing 
job is very poor. Many startups shut down within a few years. MUDRA loans are easy 
to announce, but rising NPAs show the distress at the grassroots. Youth do not want 
slogans, they want stable futures. 
Next is Federalism, Inclusion and Social Justice. True social justice is not 
achieved by centralized schemes only. State face shrinking fiscal space, delayed 
payments, and growing dependence on the Centre. Dalits, Adivasis, Minorities, 
women, and migrants need rights, representation, and resources, not just rhetoric.   
 Now, I come to the last point which is the Indian outside the Address. The

SHRI P. WILSON (Tamil Nadu) : Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, Hosur is a booming 
industrial and export hub in Tamil Nadu, a major employment generator, and a crucial 
growth engine for South India. Considering the unprecedent development, the hon.

proposal on the ground of 150-km restriction arising out of a concession agreement

Concern over decline in Siri Cow breed 
SHRI DORJEE TSHERING LEPCHA (Sikkim): Sir, the Siri Cow is not merely a 
livestock breed but it is an integral part of the agrarian culture, traditional farming 
system and rural economy of Sikkim and neighbouring Himalayan regions.                                                       
 This hardy breed is uniquely adapted to high-altitude, cold climatic 
conditions, steep terrains and organic farming practices. It plays a vital role in 
providing milk, draught power, organic manure and livelihood security to small and 
marginal farmers. However, today the Siri Cow is facing a serious threat of decline 
due to indiscriminate crossbreeding, shrinking grazing land, lack of organized 
breeding programmes, and inadequate policy support. If immediate steps are not 
taken, this valuable indigenous germplasm may be lost permanently. 
I would like to urge the Union Government to accord special recognition to the 
Siri Cow under national indigenous cattle conservation programmes, including 
Rashtriya Gokul Mission and National Livestock Mission. Dedicated Siri Cow breeding 
centres, genetic conservation units and farmer incentive schemes should be 
established in Sikkim. Support for organic dairy products, value addition and market 
linkages will further encourage farmers to continue rearing this breed.  
Preserving the Siri Cow aligns with our national objectives of biodiversity 
conservation, climate-resilient agriculture, organic farming, and rural empowerment. I 
request the Union Government to take immediate and focussed action in this regard. 
Thank you, Sir.

Concern over hiring staff in Signal and Telecommunication Department in  
Railways on contract basis 
SHRI GOLLA BABURAO (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, Safety is the biggest concern and 
there is no doubt Railways is taking various measures, including Kavach, to provide 
foolproof safety for passengers and its network. The results are encouraging – 
accidents have reduced from 135 in 2014-15 to just 31 in 2024-25.  It has all happened 
due to policies of Railways and hard work being done by regular safety category 
employees of Railways. 
But, surprisingly, Railway Board issued a Circular to GMs of 4 Railway Zones 
asking to hire people on contract to take care of modern signaling, 
telecommunications and maintenance of safety department. This move has shocked 
not only Railway Unions but also others. Safety department has complex interlock 
mechanisms and advanced electronic systems. So, contract workers, I strongly 
believe, as supervisors, field engineers and technicians may not be fully appropriate 
for train operations and passengers’ safety. Railway Board is aware that complex and 
interlocking of signal and telecom departments need high and intensive training of 
nearly 2 years at Signal & Telecommunication Training Centre (STTCs) and Indian 
Railway Institute of Signal Engineering and Telecommunications (IRISET). And, 
Commissioner of Railway Safety (CRS) in its investigation report of collision of 
Mysuru-Dharbhanga Bagmati Express flagged a similar concern. 
Hence, I appeal to the Government to withdraw the Circular to appoint 
contract workers in safety departments and, instead, appoint regular employees. 
Thank you, Sir.

Need for stronger regulatory framework for OTT Platforms 
SHRI A.D. SINGH (Bihar): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir , in recent years, Over-The-Top 
(OTT) platforms have emerged as a major medium for entertainment and information 
dissemination across India. While they have expanded creative opportunities and 
provided easy access to diverse content, several concerns have also arisen regarding 
unregulated and objectionable material being streamed on these platforms. Instances 
of content promoting violence, obscenity, communal disharmony, or disrespect to 
national and religious symbols have been reported repeatedly. 
 The Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media 
Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, prescribe a self-regulatory mechanism for OTT services; 
however, their enforcement has remained largely ineffective due to weak grievance 
redressal and lack of accountability. Many platforms continue to operate without 
proper certification or effective oversight, leading to growing public discontent and 
moral concerns. Given the widespread reach of digital media, it is essential that 
uniform standards are maintained to safeguard cultural sensitivities and public 
morality while upholding the freedom of expression. I urge the Government to review 
the existing regulatory framework, establish a statutory body to monitor OTT content, 
ensure a time-bound grievance redressal mechanism, and evolve clear guidelines for 
age classification and content warning. The Government should also consider 
consultation with all stakeholders, content creators, broadcasters, and civil society to 
create a balanced framework ensuring creative freedom while protecting social 
harmony and national interest. Thank you, Sir.

Need for effective regulation of smartphone use in schools and restrictions  on  
social media access to under-16 youth 
SHRI LAHAR SINGH SIROYA (Karnataka): Sir, I rise to highlight the growing digital 
epidemic of smartphone addiction, especially, among our school children, a threat 
experts warn is undermining focused learning, healthy social interaction, and mental 
well-being. This unchecked habit is now becoming as harmful and devastating as the 
drug menace itself, impairing concentration, social development and mental health. 
Global evidence calls for urgent action. The UNESCO Global Education Monitoring 
Report shows that nearly 100 education systems now restrict smartphones, 
recognizing that even their presence disrupts learning. Many countries across the 
world have imposed school-time bans through legislation, to restore academic focus 
and face-to-face interaction. A few other nations have prohibited users under-16 
from having social media accounts to protect them from addictive algorithms, harmful 
content, and cyber-bullying. We too need to restrict the use of smartphones and 
social media platforms.  Our current fragmented framework must be replaced with a 
firm, uniform Central legislation to ensure effective protection for every child. To 
safeguard the goals of the National Education Policy (NEP 2020), I urge the 
Government to issue an urgent Central Directive declaring all Kindergarten to 10 (K-
10) schools a 'Smartphone-Free Zone.' To address parental safety concerns, the 
Government should promote replacing smartphones with basic, voice-call-only 
feature phones ('flip phones') on campus. This is a practical and scalable solution for 
India.  We must act decisively and immediately to protect our children from this 
invisible epidemic and restore focus to our classrooms. I urge the Government to look 
into it.

Demand for integration of nutritious breakfast into the PM-POSHAN Scheme 
SHRIMATI RAJATHI (Tamil Nadu): Hon. Vice-Chairman Sir, I bring to the 
Government's attention a critical recommendation of integrating the provision of a 
nutritious breakfast, in addition to the midday meal in Government schools. Research 
consistently shows that morning hours are the most productive for learning. However, 
a significant portion of students from economically marginalized backgrounds arrive at 
school on an empty stomach. This severely impacts their concentration and academic 
outcomes. While States, like Tamil Nadu, have successfully launched the Chief 
Minister's Breakfast Scheme, benefiting lakhs of students, which shows marked 
improvement in attendance and health, many other States are unable to scale such 
initiatives due to financial constraints. 
In view of the fact that India still faces high rates of child wasting and stunting, 
this would be a necessary investment in our human capital. I, therefore, urge the 
Government to formally include breakfast in the Pradhan Mantri Poshan Shakti Nirman 
Scheme, provide a dedicated Budget for this expansion to support States, and 
provide kitchen infrastructure in Government schools to ensure safe and hygienic 
preparation of two meals per day. School meals twice a day would ensure that hunger 
does not stop children from learning and staying healthy. Thank you, Sir.

Need for tapping of Geo Thermal power 
SHRI BRIJLAL (Uttar Pradesh): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, my subject pertains to need 
for tapping geothermal power. The Prime Minister's vision for a clean and green 
energy atmanirbharta by 2040 encompasses several key areas. Energy security 
involves diversifying energy sources, boosting domestic production of alternative fuels 
like hydrogen, biofuels, solar, wind, hydro, and geothermal energy, and reducing 
dependence on imported oil and gas. Geothermal power is a new addition to it. 
[ 02 February, 2026 ]
149

Geothermal energy is heat from the earth's interior generated by radioactive decay. 
India has 381 thermally anomalous sites identified by the Geological Survey of India 
with the potential to generate 10,600 megawatts of energy, enough to power 10 
million households. ONGC is leading India's first geothermal power project in Puga 
Valley, Ladakh, with the aim of generating 1 megawatt of power in the initial phase. 
The pilot project, located at 14,000 feet, is also the world's highest geothermal power 
plant. The project will involve drilling two wells, each reaching 1,000 metres deep, to 
tap into the geothermal reservoir. 
Key projects includes a 20 kilowatt pilot plant in Manuguru, Telangana, Dirang 
in North-East, and ONGC's 1 megawatt power project in Puga Valley, Ladakh. 
Ladakh has the potential to be a commercial-scale 2,000 megawatt project in the 
future. Since Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Jammu and Kashmir, and North-East 
have many known geothermal energy spots, we should tap these sources of energy, 
which are non-polluting, carbon-free, and sustainable. The project is expected to 
provide electricity and be a great help to the forces deployed in remote and 
inhospitable terrains. I urge the Government to look into this matter. Thank you, Sir.

OBITUARY REFERENCE 
MR. CHAIRMAN:  Hon. Members, it is with profound sorrow, I inform the House about 
the passing away of Shrimati Sushila Tiriya, former Member of the Rajya Sabha on 1st 
February, 2026, at the age of 69 years. She represented  the State of Odisha from  2nd 
July, 1986 to 1st July, 1992 and again from 4th April, 2006 to 3rd April, 2012. She also 
served as a Member of the Tenth and the Eleventh Lok Sabha. 
B orn on 6th February, 1956 at Kalua-khaman  in district Mayurbhanj of Odisha, 
Shrimati Sushila Tiriya, pursued her education at Utkal University. From an early age, 
she was deeply committed to social service, particularly, for the upliftment and 
empowerment of tribal communities.  She organised tribal festivals and worked for 
safeguarding the rich traditional culture of various tribes, development of rural and tribal 
areas, and encouraging young artistes and sportspersons. 
I n the passing away of Shrimati Sushila Tiriya , the nation has lost an 
experienced legislator and a distinguished social worker. We deeply mourn the passing 
away of Shrimati Sushila Tiriya. 
 I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark of 
respect to the memory of the departed. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute.) 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Secretary-General will convey to the members of the bereaved family 
our sense of profound sorrow and deep sympathy.

Demand for including the Kothavalasa-Kirandul line in the proposed Visakhapatnam 
division of New South Coast Railway Zone 
SHRI GOLLA BABURAO (Andhra Pradesh) :  Mr. Chairman, Sir, in pursuance of the 
Andhra Pradesh (Reorganisation) Act, the Ministry of Railways is taking steps to create 
new Railway Zone in AP with Visakhapatnam as its Zonal Headquarters. Hon. PM also 
laid the foundation-stone for its headquarters, allocated money for the same last year 
and the Union Cabinet has also approved DPR for this Zone.  It is an assurance pending 
of more than 12 years and I hope that, at least, the new Zone would be notified at the 
earliest, and they would complete the construction of headquarters and provide other 
infrastructure as soon as possible to make it functional. 
 Sir, the new Zone has four divisions – Guntakal, Guntur, Vijayawada and 
Visakhapatnam.  And, all these divisions have their respective jurisdiction with different 
sections. But, Sir, I am given to understand that the Ministry of Railways is proposing 
to transfer Kothavalasa-Kirandul line from Visakhapatnam Division to Rayagada 
Division of East Coast Railway Zone, instead of keeping it within South Coast Railway 
Zone since the above line falls within the Visakhapatnam Division.  Not only this, 
Palasa-Ichchapuram sections are also proposed to transfer to new Rayagada Division 
against the wishes of the people of AP in general and North coastal AP in particular.  If 
these sections are transferred to Rayagada Division, the proposed new South Coast 
Zone becomes a mere skeleton, as this Zone is going to lose huge revenue and its 
existence would be in jeopardy. The proposed unscientific move structurally weakens 
not only Visakhapatnam Division, but also the new Zone and impacts its financial self-
sufficiency.   
In view of the above, I demand for inclusion of Kothavalasa-Kirandul and other 
lines taken to Rayagada Division be included in the Visakhapatnam Division only and 
also demand for early notification of the new South Coast Railway Zone.  Thank you.

Now, Shri A. D. Singh. 
Concern over the coastal erosion and climate displacement at India’s eastern 
coastline 
SHRI A.D. SINGH (Bihar) :  Thank you, Mr. Chairman, Sir, for giving me this 
opportunity to speak.  I rise to draw the attention of this august House to a silent but 
devastating humanitarian crisis unfolding along India's eastern coastline - coastal 
erosion and climate displacement.  As reported recently, 46 villages across 
Kendrapara, Puri and Ganjam districts of Odisha have been severely affected by coastal 
erosion.  Entire habitations like Satabhaya have been wiped off the map by the 
advancing sea.  Families, who once lived with dignity as farmers and fishers, have been 
uprooted, resettled inland and reduced to daily-wage labourers.  Safety has been 
provided to them, yes - but livelihoods have not been provided.  People relocated to 
colonies like Bagapatia live far from the sea, away from fishing grounds, agricultural 
land and markets.  Young students have dropped out of school; elderly persons are 
dependent; and women are forced into insecure work.  These are not statistics; these 
are India's first climate refugees.  
The National Centre for Coastal Research has warned that over one-third of 
India's 7,000 km coastline is eroding, with Odisha among the worst affected.  In West 
Bengal, 60 per cent of the coastline along the Digha-Shankarpur and Sundarbans is 
facing the threat of erosion.  In Tamil Nadu, 43 per cent, in Andhra Pradesh, 26 per 
cent and in Puducherry, 56 per cent of the coastline is under threat.  Rising sea levels, 
cyclones, sand mining, destruction of mangroves, ports and embankments - all 
aggravated by unplanned development - are accelerating this crisis.  If this continues, 
thousands more villages will follow Satabhaya.   
I urge the Government to act on five fronts: first, declare climate displacement a 
national policy concern; second, ensure livelihood-linked rehabilitation and not just 
housing; third, restore mangroves and natural barriers instead of relying only on 
concrete walls; fourth, strictly regulate sand mining and coastal construction; and 
[ 3 February, 2026 ]

finally, create a national climate refugee framework with dedicated funding.  The sea is 
not just eroding land; it is eroding lives.  If the Government does not act today, history 
will ask us: when India's coastal poor were drowning silently, where was the nation's 
conscience?   Thank you, Sir.

Concern over the impact of United States' tariff policies on Indian exports and 
domestic industry 
SHRI MASTHAN RAO YADAV BEEDHA (Andhra Pradesh) :   Sir, I wish to draw the 
attention of this august House to the impact of United States’ tariff policies on Indian 
exports, while also placing on record the important and positive developments 
announced on 2 nd February 2026 as well as the issues that still require clarity and 
sustained engagement.  During 2025, the United States imposed a 25 per cent 
reciprocal tariff on Indian goods, followed by an additional 25 per cent punitive duty 
linked to India's purchases of Russian oil. …(Interruptions)…  Let me complete. 
MR. CHAIRMAN:  Please don’t interfere.  Let him speak. 
SHRI MASTHAN RAO YADAV BEEDHA:  As a result, several Indian exports faced an 
effective tariff burden of 50-58 per cent, impacting nearly USD 50 billion worth of 
shipments to the U.S. market.  These measures severely disrupted trade flows, eroded 
competitiveness and created uncertainty for exporters, particularly MSMEs and labour-
intensive sectors. 
In this context, I would like to place on record my appreciation of the determined 
efforts of the hon . Prime Minister of India, Shri Narendra Modi ji, and the NDA 
Government as well as the Commerce Ministry whose proactive diplomatic 
engagement with the United States has yielded tangible results. The announcement on 
2nd February 2026 of an understanding to reduce the reciprocal tariff from 25 per cent 
to 18 per cent is a significant relief for Indian exporters and a strong signal of India's 
growing stature in global trade negotiations. The positive market response, including 
the strengthening of the Indian rupee, reflects confidence in this leadership-driven 
26
[RAJYA SABHA]

 
 
engagement.  At the same time, it is important to flag a crucial area of uncertainty.  The 
announcement so far is based on public statements and oral communication, and 
formal notification is yet to be issued under the U.S. law, including under the 
International Emergency Economic Powers Act.  Notably, President Trump's statement 
refers specifically to the reciprocal tariff and does not explicitly confirm the withdrawal 
of the additional 25 per cent punitive duty.  This distinction is evident from the U.S. 
customs entry documents, including shrimp import filings, which show two separate 
duty codes - one for the reciprocal tariff and another for the Russia-India punitive levy 
- each levied independently.  Until a formal legal clarification is issued, exporters 
continue to face uncertainty.  The shrimp industry illustrates this clearly.  Indian shrimp 
exports to the U.S. declined by around 26 per cent in late 2025 due to high tariffs.  While 
the reduction to 18 per cent restores competitiveness and offers immediate relief, a full 
revival depends on the complete removal of the punitive duty.  I, therefore, appeal to 
the Government to continue and intensify dialogue with the U.S. Administration to 
secure formal withdrawal of the punitive tariff.

Concern over the growing drug menace in the country 
SHRI JAGGESH (Karnataka): Sir, my subject is concern over growing drug menace 
threatening India's youth. The escalating drug violence in our country poses a grave 
threat to public health, public safety and the future of our youth. Across India, drug 
abuse and trafficking are spreading rapidly, particularly among students and young 
professionals. Synthetic drugs are increasingly circulated through organized inter-State 
and international networks, exploiting urban centres and digital platforms. Within this 
national crisis, Bangalore stands out as a particular concerning example. As a major 
metropolitan city and a technology hub, it has witnessed a sharp rise in drug 
consumption and trafficking. Educational institutions, workplaces, entertainment hubs 
and residential areas have become prime targets for drug syndicates, highlighting the 
[ 3 February, 2026 ]
27

 
 
urgent need for stronger intelligence, preventive policy and coordinated enforcement. 
The impact of drug abuse goes far beyond the individual. It devastates family, leads to 
financial hardships, domestic conflicts and lasting emotional trauma. It fuels crime, 
mental illness, road accidents, workplace inefficiency and broader social instability. 
Despite this risk, conviction rates remain low, exposing gaps in investigation and 
prosecution while rehabilitation, counselling and awareness programmes remain 
insufficient. Effectiveness of our national response is further weakened when certain 
State Governments, including Karnataka, fail to demonstrate sustained commitment 
and seriousness in tackling this menace. A comprehensive and decisive approach is 
required, combining strict enforcement with widespread awareness, early intervention 
and accessible de-addiction rehabilitation.  
I urge the Government to spearhead a strong national movement against drug 
abuse and trafficking with coordinated action, strict enforcement and robust support 
system to safeguard our youth, protect families and strengthen the society as whole. 
Thank you.

Concern over the unregulated access of children to social media and smartphones 
SHRI SANJAY KUMAR JHA (Bihar): Sir, I rise to draw the urgent attention of this House 
to the unregulated exposure of children to social media. In 2025, Australia enacted a 
law prohibiting under-16s from major platforms after a study showed 96 per cent of 
children aged 10-15 use social media and seven in ten encountered harmful content.  
In India, a 2025 Local Circles study found that 82 per cent of children aged 14-
16 can operate smart phones, only 57 per cent use them mainly for education and 76 
per cent access social media research. Research indicates 11-37 per cent show 
problematic use, causing language and communication setbacks, social and emotional 
learning delays, poor motor development, disrupted sleep and reduced focus. 
As countries worldwide evolve policy to regulate children’s exposure to social 
media, I strongly support deliberation in this House to curb excessive screen time 
among toddlers, pre-teenagers and teenagers. This is because the current literature 
on screen-time exposure and child development broadly suggests that excessive 
[ 3 February, 2026 ]
33

 
 
screen use in early childhood is negatively associated with developmental outcome 
among children. While digital classrooms were unavoidable during pandemic, parents 
and school administration must actively monitor duration and content quality.  
According to the Indian Academy of Pediatrics Guidelines on Screen Time Among 
Children, very early exposure to screen-based media and excessive screen time seems 
to be widely prevalent among Indian children. Also, a new study published based on 
the survey of 3,624 parents across five Indian States found that screen exposure among 
children aged two to five years far exceeds the World Health Organization guidelines. 
Such findings underscore the need for timely safeguard to protect development 
outcome.  To begin with, smart phone being ubiquitous device in Indian households 
with over 85 per cent of Indian households owning smart phones, their use by children 
merit regulation. The House may consider, specifically, debating whether smart phone 
packs would carry a statutory use advisory. The Economic Survey 2025-2026 has 
flagged a rapid rise of digital addiction and screen-related mental health problem as a 
major healthcare issue, particularly, among children and adolescents. A timely 
intervention to safeguard the developmental milestone of India’s adolescents is 
essential to leverage India’s demographic dividend in realizing the goals of Viksit Bharat 
2047.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS  
International expansion of UPI 
*31. DR. MEDHA VISHRAM KULKARNI: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the number of countries where the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) is currently 
operational or linked with local payment systems; 
(b) the total transaction value and volume carried out through international UPI 
linkages during the last three years, year-wise:  
(c) whether Government has conducted any assessment of UPI's role in enhancing 
India's digital payment leadership globally; and  
(d) the future roadmap for expanding UPI to additional countries, particularly for the 
benefit of Indian diaspora and international trade? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PANKAJ 
CHAUDHARY): (a) to (d): A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
38
[RAJYA SABHA]

 
 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Unified Payment Interface (UPI) is currently working in 8 countries 
i.e. Bhutan, France, Mauritius, Nepal, Qatar, Singapore, Sri Lanka and UAE. The year-
wise transactions (both value and volume) reported during the last three financial years 
are as under: 
Financial Year Volume (Actuals) Value ( ₹Lakhs) 
2023-24              37,060            1,970 
2024-25            755,445        25,853  
2025-26*          1,486,537        33,043  
*Till December 2025 
(c) and (d)  The Government, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and NPCI 
International Payments Ltd. (NIPL) have been taking up various steps for international 
expansion of Unified Payment Interface (UPI). These inter-alia, include 
operationalisation of UPI linkages with comparable fast payment systems of partner 
countries to facilitate cross ‑border person ‑to‑person (P2P) remittance flows, as well 
as the establishment of travel ‑based corridors to enable cross ‑border 
person‑to‑merchant (P2M) payments. Further, NIPL is offering the UPI technology 
stack to interested partner countries for development of sovereign, real-time digital 
payment systems similar to UPI. 
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) report on ‘Growing Retail Digital 
Payments (The Value of Interoperability)’ dated June 2025 has recognized UPI as the 
world’s largest retail fast-payment system by transaction volume. Further, as per ACI 
Worldwide report 2024, UPI accounts for around 49% of transaction volumeof the

Adverse effects of excessive salt consumption 
*32. SHRI MUKUL BALKRISHNA WASNIK : Will the MINISTER OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a)   whether excessive salt consumption has emerged as a critical health crisis in 
India, primarily driving a 'silent pandemic' of Hypertension and Cardiovascular 
diseases; 
42
[RAJYA SABHA]

 
 
(b)    if so, the details thereof and steps taken by Government to promote awareness 
about the ill-effects of excessive salt consumption ; 
(c)    whether it is a fact that consumption of Low Sodium Salt Substitutes (LSS) can 
go a long way in combating this 'silent pandemic' ; and 
(d)   if so, the action taken by Government to ensure accessibility and affordability of 
LSSs? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY  
WELFARE (SHRI PRATAPRAO JADHAV): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the 
Table of the House.  
Statement  
(a) to (d) As per Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), excessive salt 
consumption is a contributor to the growing burden of hypertension and cardiovascular 
diseases.   
The Government of India, through the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India 
(FSSAI), is implementing the  Eat Right India  movement to promote healthy eating 
practices and awareness about the harmful effects of excessive salt consumption. 
Under this movement, key activities include: 
   Mass media and social media campaigns such as “Aaj Se ThodaKam”  to 
encourage gradual reduction in salt, sugar and fat intake in daily diet.  
   Development and dissemination of the Eat Right Toolkit  for frontline health 
workers to counsel communities on limiting high fat, sugar and salt (HFSS) foods.  
Based on a review of the available evidence on effects and safety, and consideration of 
additional contextual factors, WHO in 2025 recommended: 
  To reduce blood pressure and the risk of cardiovascular diseases, it is 
recommended to reduce sodium intake to less than 2 gm/day (strong 
recommendation). 
[ 3 February, 2026 ]
43

 
 
   In this context, using less regular table salt is an important part of an overall 
sodium reduction strategy. If choosing to use table salt, WHO suggests replacing 
regular table salt with lower-sodium substitutes that contain potassium (conditional 
recommendation). This recommendation is intended for adults (not pregnant women 
or children) in general populations, excluding individuals with kidney impairments or 
with other circumstances or conditions that might compromise potassium excretion.

MR. CHAIRMAN:  Now, Question No.34. 
Ayush Nivesh Saarthi 
*34. SHRIMATI SEEMA DWIVEDI: Will the Minister of AYUSH be pleased to state; 
 (a)    the outcomes achieved in facilitating investment through platforms such as 
AYUSH Invest Saarthi; 
(b)    he details of operational projects, participation of micro, small and medium 
enterprise (MSMEs) and employment generation thereunder; 
[ 3 February, 2026 ]
55

 
 
(c)    the major countries contributing to foreign direct investment (FDI) and research 
and development (R and D) collaboration in the AYUSH sector; 
(d)     whether there has been an increase in exports of AYUSH medicines and products 
under the AYUSH Invest Saarthi Platform; and  
(e)     if so, the details of the major countries importing AYUSH medicines and products 
under the said platform?  
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF AYUSH  (SHRI PRATAPRAO 
JADHAV): (a) to (e) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Ministry of Ayush has launched Ayush Nivesh Saarthi portal on 29th May 
2025 which aims to boost traditional medicine systems as a strong economic sector of 
the country. The portal has acted as a comprehensive investment facilitation platform, 
promoting opportunities in Ayush sector. It serves as a global hub for information 
related to trade in medicinal plants, derivatives and extracts and supports the growing 
export market for Ayush products encouraging research and development as well as 
collaborations between industry and academia. 
Through Ayush Nivesh Saarthi Portal, Ministry of Ayush has consolidated 
existing policy frameworks and incentive structures, showcased investment ready 
projects and facilitated real time investor engagement under one unified interface. 
(b) The Ayush Nivesh Saarthi Portal is primarily an investment facilitation and 
information dissemination platform, while it does not directly implement or monitor 
operational projects, the portal provides information and guidance to a wide range of 
stakeholders, including Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs), by 
showcasing investment opportunities, relevant policies, schemes and Ayush Statistics. 
(c) Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) up to 100% is permitted through the 
automatic route in the Ayush sector, encouraging global investment. Majorly FDI in 
Ayush sector has been received from countries like Mauritius, Singapore, France and 
Malaysia. 
56
[RAJYA SABHA]

 
 
Ministry of Ayush has signed 27 Country to Country MoUs for Cooperation in 
field of Traditional Medicine, 54 Institute to Institute level MoUs with foreign institutes 
for undertaking Collaborative Research/Academic collaboration. The details are 
attached at Annexure-A and Annexure-B respectively.  
(e) and (e) The Ayush Nivesh Saarthi Portal serves as an investment facilitation and 
trade promotion platform. While the portal itself does not directly track or attribute 
export figures to individual transactions, its launch has strengthened visibility of the 
Ayush sector in global markets and supported exporters through dissemination of 
country-wise market intelligence, standards, and incentive schemes. Major importing 
countries of Ayush medicines and products, include the United States of America, 
European Union countries, United Arab Emirates, France, Russia, UK, and South-East 
Asian nations as per data available withDirectorate General of Commercial Intelligence 
and Statistics (DGCI and S), Ministry of Commerce and Industry.

Now, Question No. 35. 
Regulating prices of pharmaceutical drugs 
35. MS. SWATI MALIWAL : Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be 
pleased to state: 
(a)   whether any consultations or policy reviews are underway for capping or regulating 
prices of pharmaceutical drugs, particularly high-cost and life-saving medicines, 
beyond those covered under National List of Essential Medicines;  
(b)  whether National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority has examined or recommended 
expansion of price controls, trade margin rationalisation or other regulatory 
measures for non-scheduled drugs and emerging high-cost therapies;  
(c)     whether representations have been received from public health experts, patient 
groups, committees or State Governments seeking wider drug price regulation 
and action taken thereon; and 
[ 3 February, 2026 ]
71

 
 
(d)     whether Government proposes to review Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, to 
strengthen affordability? 
THE MINISTER IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI JAGAT 
PRAKASH NADDA: (a) to (d): A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Consultations on policy issues are an ongoing and transparent activity 
which is undertaken by the Department to assess the relevance, impact and efficiency 
of the existing policy reform required, if any, keeping in view the interest of all 
stakeholders.  The Department and National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) 
has held consultation with various stakeholder with pharmaceutical industry 
associations like CII, FICCI, OPPI, IPA, AIMED, ADVAMED, MTAI, USIBC, 
ASSOCHAM, NATHEALTH etc., MSMEs Association like LaghuUdhyog Bharti, IDMA, 
FOPE, Patient advocacy groups like AIDAN, MSF, Patient Safety and access initiative 
of India Foundation. etc., on the matters concerning National Pharmaceuticals Pricing 
Policy, 2012 (NPPP, 2012) and Drug (Prices Control) Order, 2013 (DPCO, 2013).  
Feedbacks were received from the stakeholders on the operation of the existing policy 
framework. These suggestions/ feedbacks received during such consultations provide 
stakeholders input on issues requiring redressal in the existing policy, if any. The 
Department and NPPA remain engaged with stakeholders with a view to understanding 
issues and resolving them either under extant mechanism or by making appropriate 
provision. 
(d) Review of DPCO, 2013 is a continuous process which is done periodically 
by the Department or as and when required to ensure that the provisions of DPCO, 
2013 are enforced effectively so that the essential drugs are made accessible and 
available to the public at affordable price.

Home-based physiotherapy services for paralysis/stroke patients 
#*36 SHRIMATI DARSHANA SINGH : Will the MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a)     whether access to regular physiotherapy treatment for patients suffering from 
stroke or paralysis is limited in the country, particularly in rural and remote 
areas; 
(b)     whether any special programme or financial assistance scheme is proposed to 
provide home-based treatment to stroke/paralysis patients and to improve 
access to health care services in future, if so, the details thereof; and 
(c)  whether there is any plan to enhance the availability of home-physiotherapy 
equipment such as tools, stretching bands and mobile rehabilitation kits 
through Public Private Partnership? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY  
WELFARE (SHRI PRATAPRAO JADHAV): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table 
of the House.  
Statement  
(a) Health is a State Subject. The Department of Health and Family Welfare, 
Government of India provides technical and financial support to the States and Union 
Territories under the National Health Mission (NHM) to strengthen public health care 
system.  
Under the National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly (NPHCE), 
rehabilitation services, including physiotherapy, are provided for elderly patients with 
functional limitations, including those suffering from stroke or paralysis.  
 
# Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.  
78
[RAJYA SABHA]

 
 
 (b) Financial assistance is provided to States/UTs for implementation of 
services including physiotherapy under NPHCE as per approved Programme 
Implementation Plans (PIPs). 
Further, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has implemented the National 
Programme for Palliative Care (NPPC) under the National Health Mission since 2013 to 
support patients with chronic and debilitating condition, including stroke and paralysis 
patients. 
(c)  The State Governments are given technical and financial support under 
NHM to enhance the availability of physiotherapy services. Since health is a State 
Subject, the mode of implementation is decided by the State/UT Governments.

THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI TIRUCHI SIVA) :  Thank you, Ranjeet ji, you have 
concluded within your time.  I appreciate that.  Next speaker is hon. Member, Ms. Dola 
Sen, not present.  Next speaker is hon. Member, Dr. Vikramjit Singh Sahney, not 
present.  Next speaker is hon. Member, Shri S Niranjan Reddy.                                                             
SHRI S NIRANJAN REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I rise to reflect 
on the hon. President's Address. The Address reflects India’s confident assertion and 
transition into the second phase of 21 st Century with emphasis on technology-led 
128
[RAJYA SABHA]

 
 
growth, infrastructure expansion and inclusive development.  Sir, while I represent the 
State of Andhra Pradesh, this vision aligns with the State's dual character as a 
technology hub and agrarian coastal economy.  The hon. President's Address deals 
with all these aspects with sufficient details. I want to focus on one aspect that the hon. 
President's Address refers to, namely, the Government moving forward on the path of 
reforms express.  In the reforms’ express that the Government is embarked on, I find 
that there are certain other bogies that may need to be attached to this particular 
express. While various areas have been covered, I want to focus on two or three 
specific areas. The first one is on technology and digital economy. India’s progress in 
the digital economy is evident from the electronics production crossing rupees 11 lakh 
crore. Smartphone exports exceeding rupees one lakh crore in early 2025-26. Large-
scale AI skilling creates significant opportunities for Southern States like Andhra 
Pradesh and Telangana that host IT, GCCs, electronics and data center ecosystems. 
However, the expansion has exposed certain structural gaps. India's National 
Cybersecurity Policy dates back to 2013 which predates the scale of cloud computing, 
data centers, and AI-driven systems, critical digital public infrastructure, and 
underscoring the need for a modernized cybersecurity framework. At the same time, 
the industry estimates point to a substantial shortage of skilled professionals in 
emerging areas, such as cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, semiconductor design, 
and advanced electronics despite ongoing training initiatives. I note with satisfaction 
that the hon. President's Address refers to the necessity of increasing the skilling and 
also providing for education in these sectors from an earlier stage.

 Madam Vice-Chairman, I am equally happy to state that significant focus and 
attention on livestock and dairy development has been given in the Address.  India’s 
fisheries sector, especially, coastal and marine fisheries, has also witnessed 
unprecedented policy support.  I am sure that these measures will go a long way and 
they will be the stakeholders in India’s economic growth in the future.  Across all the

SHRI NIRANJAN BISHI (Odisha):  Thank you, Vice Chairperson Madam. I offer my 
profound thanks for allowing me to speak on the Motion of Thanks to the hon. 
President's Address. Her Excellency, the President, is from our soil of Odisha; she is

our pride and glory. She belongs to our tribal community. We, the 15 crore tribal people 
of the tribal society in India, are very proud.  But Sir, currently, the tribal people in India 
are not safe. There are attacks on the land, water, and forests of the tribals. There are 
attacks on the education, health, socio-economic, and cultural rights of the tribals, as 
well as on their constitutional rights. Our ANWESHA scheme, our UGC, our 
scholarships, our stipends, our reservation in appointments, reservation in promotions, 
and reservation in political posts—everything is being diluted. The Atrocities Act is 
being diluted. Reservation is being gradually diluted. Recently, our hon. Union 
Education Minister had brought a very good system and a very good law through the 
UGC for the protection of our ST, SC, OBC, and women; India welcomed it, but it was 
stayed through various means. 
  Madam, in our universities, there are no ST or SC lecturers, readers, professors, 
or associate professors; hundreds of posts are lying vacant. It is necessary that the 
UGC implements measures to fill them. On the other hand, posts for ST and SC remain 
vacant in the High Courts and the Supreme Court as well. The Government should fill 
those posts through a Special Recruitment Drive; the Her Excellency the President 
should have mentioned this in her Address.  Madam, in Odisha, the former Chief 
Minister Shri Naveen Patnaik had initiated a beautiful scheme called the 'Anvesha' 
Urban Education scheme. Under this, ST and SC children could study the CBSE 
pattern course completely free of charge. That has been closed since January 25th; it 
remains closed even on January 26th.  Naveen Babu had established Odisha Adarsha 
Vidyalayas in 314 blocks and had started the NMMS scholarship scheme providing a 
stipend of 12,000 rupees. In those schools, ST, SC, rural OBC, and General students 
all studied. The admission which was from Standard 1 to Plus Two, that too is being 
closed. So, instead of things doubling in the 'Double Engine' Government, they are 
being shut down. Her Excellency said nothing on this matter.

first, and then treatment happens. But the ST, SC, OBC, women, farmers, and the

SHRI MAHARAJA SANAJAOBA LEISHEMBA (Manipur): Thank you Madam for giving 
me the opportunity to participate in the discussion on “Motion of Thanks on the Hon. 
President’s Address to both the Houses on 28 th January, 2026. ”  On behalf of the 
North-East people, I would like to express my heartfelt gratitude and thanks to our hon. 
President of India and hon. Prime Minister, Shri Narendra Modi for their great concerns 
and inclusiveness of North-Eastern Region with the rest of the country.  In her Address, 
hon. President stated in her speech that “2026” would be the foundational year for Viksit 
Bharat by 2047.  The nation celebrates with great honour (i) 150 years of Vande 
Mataram; (ii) 350th Martyrdom Day of Guru Tegh Bahadur; (iii) 150th Birth Anniversaries 
of Bhagwan Birsa Munda and Sardar Patel.    These milestones remind us of our rich 
heritage and sacrifices of our ancestors and inspire further momentum to our journey 
towards Viksit Bharat by 2047. 
 As I belong to North-East Region, where the dalits, the backward (pichhda), 
the deprived (vanchit) and the tribal communities settle dominantly, I would like to give 
more focus on North-East.  Our Government’s commitment is “Sabka Sath, Sabka 
[ 3 February, 2026 ]
149

 
 
Vikas”:  (i) A decisive battle against major diseases like ‘Sickle Cell Anemia’ has been 
fought to save our tribal people.  Over 6.5 crore tribal citizens have already been 
screened; (ii) More than 400 Eklavya Model Residential Schools have been opened in 
tribal areas to avail quality education and better future for our tribal children; (iii) In the 
last 11 years, post-metric scholarships of more than Rs.42,000 crore have been given 
to Scheduled Tribe students and about 5 crore students have benefited from this 
initiative.    
 Under the leadership of hon. Prime Minister, the North-East Region is 
empowering as the “Growth Engine of India. ”  Due to the negligent approach of the 
then UPA Government towards the Region, the North-East was pushed towards 
instability and underdevelopment.  But with the vision of “Purvodaya”, our Government 
is ensuring ‘Inclusive Growth for the Region’, transforming it as ‘Growth Engine of India’ 
and bringing long-term stability in the Region.   
Under the Modiji’s Government, North-East has received unprecedented focus.  
One, under the PM Gram Sadak Yojana, 50,000 rural roads have been constructed for 
easy access to markets, schools and offices etc..  Second, for Manipur also, a total 
special assistance of Rs.3,356 crores from 2020 till January, 2026 (under Special 
Assistance to States for Capital Expenditure) is provided to the State in the form of 50 
years’ interest-free loans; interest costs are borne by Central Government entirely.                                                         
Number three, investment of Rs. 80,000 crores in Railways has brought broad-
gauge connectivity to Arunachal Pradesh, Tripura and Mizoram. Manipur was also 
connected with broad-gauge Railways network at Jiribam for passenger train in May, 
2016, and first goods train reached Rani Gaidinliu Railway Station, Tamenglong, 
Manipur in 2022. If the pending works, that is, from Rani Gaidinliu Station to Imphal is 
completed at the earliest, then Manipur will be included in Railways Map of India. By 
the way, Imphal Railway Station is also being constructed under Amrit Bharat Station 
Scheme.  
Number four is, a large health infrastructure and development project being 
prepared in the region, like (a) construction of a medical college in Sikkim, (b) a 
women and child hospital in Agartala, (c) a medical college worth Rs. 46 crore at 
Churachandpur District, Manipur, has already been inaugurated by hon. Home 
150
[RAJYA SABHA]

 
 
Minister, Shri Amit Shahji, and (d) Assam will soon become a lifeline for semiconductor 
chips.   Thus, Purvodaya is fast transforming the North-East into a resilient growth 
engine of Viksit Bharat. Recently, on 13 th September 2025, our hon. Prime Minister 
dedicated the following major projects during his visit to Manipur. (1) New Civil 
Secretariat at Imphal-East Manipur for enhancing governance infrastructure. (2) IT-
SEZ building and new Police Headquarters at Imphal-East Manipur for expanding 
technology and security infrastructure. (3) Manipur Bhawans in Delhi and Kolkata for 
providing accommodation support for citizens from the State. (4) Ima Markets in four 
districts, establishing dedicated economic space for women traders of Manipur . (5) 
Imphal Airport, i. e., Bir Tikendrajit International Airport has been covered under Krishi 
Udan Scheme to assist farmers in transporting agricultural products, and (6) For 
developing tourism, over Rs. 117 crore has been sanctioned under Swadesh Darshan 
Scheme in Manipur. 
I once again express my heartfelt gratitude to the hon. President and the hon. 
Prime Minister for transforming the North-East region, including Manipur, into a resilient 
growth engine of India, to become Viksit Bharat by 2047.  With these few words, I 
conclude my speech on the Motion of Thanks on the President's address. Thank you, 
Madam.

parties to rise  above politics to protect national security, electoral integrity and dignity 
of democracy.

SHRI P. P. SUNEER (Kerala): Thank you, Madam, for giving me this opportunity to 
speak on the Motion of Thanks to the President's Address on behalf of my Party, the 
Communist Party of India. Disagreement is the soul of democracy. It is with that spirit 
that I rise to strongly differ several assertions made in the President’s Address, which, 
in my view, fail to reflect the lived realities of our people. The Sarkaria Commission 
reminded us that federalism is a basic feature of our Constitution. Yet, today, States 
like Kerala are forced to approach Courts even for disaster relief. Borrowing ceilings, 
delayed dues and arbitrary fiscal rules amount to a financial blockade. The Centre 
appears to be adopting a coercive approach towards opposition-ruled States, forcing 
neo-liberal policies and even withholding education funds to enforce compliance. The 
States like Kerala are facing extraordinary fiscal stress and they require immediate and 
substantial Central intervention and support. Federalism is not a favour from the Centre; 
it is a constitutional mandate.  
On labour reforms, the Government has dismissed over 29 Central labour laws, 
replacing them with four Labour Codes without meaningful consultation with workers. 
This is not reform; it is rollback. These changes weaken job security, dilute social 
protection and tilt the balance decisively against labour in favour of capital. Jobless 
growth, rising unemployment, skyrocketing price rise, widening inequality, widespread 
contractualisatiion of labour, insecurity and denial of the fundamental right to live are all 
what the last decade of the BJP regime has brought to the people.                                                            
Sir, the Economic Survey 2025-26 has suggested a “re-examination” of the 
Right to Information Act, 2005, enacted by the UPA-1 Government along with the 
MGNREGA, which marked a historic advance in institutionalizing transparency and 
democratic accountability.  The RTI framework has already been systematically 
weakened over the past decade by this Government.  Amendments enacted in 2019 
undermined the independence of the Information Commissions by placing the tenure 
and service conditions of the Information Commissioners at the discretion of the Central 
[ 3 February, 2026 ]
161

 
 
Government.  Procedural changes to the RTI rules have made information harder to 
access.  Any further dilution of the RTI Act would be disastrous for democratic 
accountability and public trust. 
 On foreign    policy, lofty claims   of balance and vision ring hollow when India 
remains largely silent on major humanitarian crises- from Ukraine, Gaza to Venezuela.  
India's   approach is in a state of complete paralysis*  
Lately, the announcement and promotion of the so-called ‘Board of Peace’ as 
a peace initiative by Donald Trump, in reality, undermines the central role of the United 
Nations - the only universally-recognized body entrusted with upholding international 
law and sovereign equality of nations. The record of the Trump administration towards 
the United Nations exposes the real intent behind the ‘Board of Peace’.  During his 
tenure, the U.S. has withdrawn from 66 international organisations, out of which 31 are 
linked to the United Nations involved in activities such as climate change, international 
solar alliance, WHO, UN Human Rights Council, etc.

SHRI P. P. SUNEER:  Now, I conclude. The Indian Government should condemn such 
actions of the United States and we should reject the invitation to join the ‘Board of 
Peace’.  Strategic ambiguity cannot substitute moral leadership. Thank you, Madam.

MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN:  Dr. Sarfraz Ahmad, not present. Shri S. Selvaganabathy. 
SHRI S. SELVAGANABATHY (Puducherry):  Hon. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I am happy 
to extend my heartfelt gratitude to the hon. President for the inspiring Address to both 
the Houses of Parliament.  Her words reflect the aspirations of a billion citizens and the 
vision of a nation marching confidently towards a brighter future.  In supporting the 
Motion of Thanks, I wish to highlight some of the important points that define our 
collective journey.  Ensuring dignity for gareeb through inclusive growth, under the 
leadership of hon. Prime Minister, Shri Narendra Modi, the Government has focused 
on freeing the gareeb from the vicious cycle of poverty and enabling them to progress 
with dignity.  As a result of targeted and transparent welfare schemes, nearly 25 crore 
Indians have risen out of poverty.  Reflecting this commitment, over 4 crore pakka 
houses have been built for the poor in the last decade, including 32 lakhs in the last 
year.  Through the Jal Jeevan Mission, piped drinking water has reached 12.5 crore 
new families in five years, with one crore added in the last year alone.  More than 10 
crore households have also received LPG connection under the Ujjwala Yojana.  By 
eliminating leakages through DBT, the Government has ensured direct, corruption-free 
delivery of benefit worth Rs.6.75 lakh crore, transforming welfare into empowerment 
and laying the foundation for a more inclusive and aspirational India.                                       
The Modi Government aims at holistic welfare of our annadatas, that is, our farmers, 
and anchors Viksit Bharat on annadata’s prosperity, positioning agriculture as the 
institutional foundation of national development. A testament to this commitment is the 
transfer of rupees four lakh crore directly to farmers’ accounts, establishing measurable 
income security under PM Kisan Accounts. 
The Modi Government honours the honest taxpayer.  For decades, the middle-
class, 31 per cent of India's population, slaved as the silent engine of growth. They 
worked the hardest, yet the UPA Government mercilessly trapped even low-income 
families in the tax net with a pitiful exemption of rupees two lakh. Families were blood-
dry, dreams were deferred, and aspirations were crushed under heavy burdens.

Today, the current policy has made annual income up to rupees twelve lakh completely 
tax-free. This is a prosperity premium introduced by the Modi Government that puts 
back thousands of rupees into the pockets of over 3.3 crore salaried citizens every 
month. 
While earlier taxpayers were burdened by a rigid two-year window for 
corrections, the timeline for updating income tax returns has now been doubled to four 
years. Similarly, the TDS threshold on rent has been increased from Rs. 2.4 lakh to Rs. 
6 lakh. This is not mere relief; it is justice for the honest taxpayer, ending the UPA's era 
of exploitation and fuelling the aspirations of every young professional, home buyer, 
and parents. 
Now, I come to education for all.  From scarcity to holistic excellence, the middle 
class is no longer forced to settle for a stagnant education system defined by the 
scarcity mindset of the Congress and the rote learning methods of the pre-2014 era. 
For over six decades, before 2014, successive Congress Governments presided over 
chronic neglect, adding just a handful of seven AIIMS in 60 years and barely expanding 
medical colleges to mere 387, leaving millions of aspiring doctors and middle-class 
families in despair. 
In contrast, under Prime Minister Narendra Modi's bold vision, we have 
shattered those barriers, and the number of AIIMS has been increased to 23, which is 
more than tripple; medical colleges have nearly been doubled to 808. Undergraduate 
medical students have surged by 141 per cent and postgraduate students by 144 per 
cent. Universities have jumped from 723 to 1168 in the last decade.  From launching the 
PM Vidyalakshmi scheme for student financial aid to providing one crore internship 
opportunities in top companies, the focus has shifted from just granting degrees to 
creating a future-ready workforce for Viksit Bharat. 
My next point is about engineering sovereignty and global benchmark.  The Modi 
Government's guarantee to a Viksit Bharat by 2047 is visible in the rapid delivery of 
engineering marvels across our diverse landscape, from the Chenab Bridge, the 
world's highest railway bridge in Jammu and Kashmir, to the Atal Tunnel in Himachal 
Pradesh and the Atal Setu in Mumbai. In stark contrast, the Congress-led UPA era was

ground-breaking 72.5 meter navigational span that rises vertically 17 meters in just five

symbolizing a nation that no longer just dreams but delivers world-class infrastructure. 
 As regards restoring cultural pride and spiritual connectivity, guided by the

Concern over the rising incidences of crimes and the erosion of public safety in 
Society 
DR. SASMIT PATRA (Odisha):  Madam, I draw the attention of the Government to a 
deeply troubling national trend which is the steady rise in violent crimes, gender-based 
offences and targeted attacks on vulnerable communities, leading to a serious erosion 
of public safety and constitutional assurance.  While policing is primarily a State subject, 
the nature, scale and persistence of such crimes, and their direct bearing on 
fundamental rights, internal security, and the implementation of Central laws and 
schemes, make this an issue that warrants the attention of the Central Government. 
Over the past two years, multiple cases of heinous crimes against women and 
girl children, including sexual violence, have shaken public conscience and exposed 
serious gaps in prevention, child protection and timely justice. There have also been 
[ 3 February, 2026 ]
189

repeated reports of violence, intimidation and social coercion against Scheduled 
Tribes, Scheduled Castes and minorities raising concerns about the effective 
enforcement of constitutional safeguards and special protection laws. 
Instances of gang violence, murders and communal tensions point not merely 
to isolated failures, but to systemic weaknesses in early intervention, investigation and 
accountability. Such conditions undermine public confidence in institutions and 
weaken social harmony, which is essential for development and national integration. 
I, therefore, urge the Union Government to (a) strengthen the implementation 
of laws relating to crimes against women and children, including fast track courts and 
victim support and (b) ensure effective enforcement of protections for Scheduled 
Tribes, Scheduled Castes and minorities.

Demand for Establishment of a branch of Central Board of Film 
 Certification (CBFC) in Gujarat 
SHRI KESRIDEVSINH JHALA (Gujarat):  Madam, I bring to draw the attention of the 
Government to the remarkable rise and contributions of the Gujarati Film Industry to 
Indian cinema. Historically, Gujarati entrepreneurs, producers, directors and actors 
have played an essential role in shaping the cinematic landscape of our country.       
Thanks to the progressive policies of the Gujarat Government and ongoing 
technological advancements, the Gujarati film sector has witnessed rapid growth. From 
releasing just 10–20 films annually, the industry now produces over 75 films each year, 
with annual investments surpassing Rs.150 crore. Further, around 125–150 Censor 
Certificates are issued annually for a diverse range of content, including feature films, 
advertisements, short films, documentaries and web content. However, at present, 
Gujarati producers and Preview Committee members are compelled to travel to 
Mumbai and other locations for CBFC screenings. This results in significant logistical 
and financial strain. The establishment of a CBFC branch in Gujarat, ideally in 
190
[RAJYA SABHA]

Ahmedabad or Gandhinagar, would greatly benefit all stakeholders by ensuring timely 
processing, reducing travel costs and easing the burden on the Mumbai office. 
Moreover, such a branch could extend its services to contents in Kutchhi, Sindhi and 
potentially Rajasthani-Marwadi languages, thereby enhancing cultural representation 
from the region. Under the visionary leadership of hon. Prime Minister, Gujarat has set 
benchmarks in several sectors, and it is now poised to lead in cinematic infrastructure 
as well.  
I, therefore, urge the Government to kindly expedite the process of establishing 
a branch of CBFC at Ahmedabad or Gandhinagar at the earliest. Thank you.

Demand for implementation of a National Road Safety Mission 
SHRI TIRUCHI SIVA (Tamil Nadu) : Madam, road safety is a multifaceted challenge, 
spanning policing, public health, social behaviour, and urban planning and mobility. 
Adequate attention is required to be paid to these sectors. The Supreme Court has 
flagged that electronic enforcement standards need to be implemented, but little action 
has been taken in this regard. Ambulance availability and emergency preparedness vary 
widely, especially in rural areas. The lack of timely trauma care often leads to 
preventable deaths. Separate initiatives focusing on road safety currently exist, 
undertaken by Central and local authorities. However, such patchwork legislation and 
fragmented strategy have yielded weak results. The number of road accidents and their 
severity has been steadily increasing. In 2024 alone, 1.77 lakh people have died in road 
accidents, which average to about 485 persons a day. More than 4.6 lakh people have 
been injured in 2023. Over-speeding is responsible for 7 in 10 of these deaths.   
India’s road accident fatality rate stands at 11.89 per 1, 00, 000 people. This 
poses a great economic burden of roughly three per cent of the country’s GDP annually. 
[ 3 February, 2026 ]
191

Against this backdrop, human-centric interventions– which prioritize pedestrian 
safety, public transportation and strengthen trauma care facilities – are essential. 
Coordinated efforts across agencies, alongside strict enforcement of traffic laws, could 
save many lives. I urge the Government to establish and implement a National Road 
Safety Mission. Thank you.
